newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government rebuked on immigration law.
newsitem.headline: French government rebuked on immigration law.

text.p: France's Constitutional Council on Wednesday watered down a controversial new law clamping down on immigration.

But hardline Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre brushed off the setback, saying the core of the new law, bitterly contested by the opposition Socialist party, was cleared by the constitutional watchdog.
"This is a success for the government," he said.
The Council threw out one provision allowing police access to the fingerprints of applicants for political asylum, ruling that it breached the constitution.

It rejected a second provision allowing authorities to refuse to renew a 10-year residence permit for any foreigner whose presence was deemed a danger to public order. It ruled that anyone in France for a decade had a right to family life in the country.
"We again have the proof that the Debre law is not only inappropriate and inefficient, but also dangerous," said Socialist deputy Julien Dray.
But the Interior Ministry said the annulments would not affect the bill's central drive to tighten controls, mainly aimed at non-European immigrants, and to crack down on illegal workers.

The new law will still, for instance, let authorities take fingerprints of asylum seekers, allow police to retain passports of illegal immigrants and double the maximum first period of detention for immigrants awaiting deportation to 48 hours.
The Interior Ministry said both the rejected provisions had been introduced as amendments to the original bill when it was passed last month by the conservative-dominated parliament.

President Jacques Chirac on Monday dissolved the National Assembly and called an election for May 25-June 1, saying France needed to revitalise itself and to enter a European single currency in 1999 from a position of strength.

The Socialists had sought to have the entire law declared unconstitutional, saying it violated French traditions of hospitality and pandered to the extreme-right National Front party of Jean-Marie Le Pen.
Le Pen wants to expel three million immigrants.

The European parliament had urged France to withdraw the bill in a resolution on xenophobia, sparking angry denunciations by Paris that the Strasbourg-based group was meddling in internal French affairs.

After a spate of protests by film-makers, artists, writers and academics, the government in February withdrew the most controversial clause of the bill that would have obliged hosts to report the departure of foreign guests.

The government says the bill closes loopholes in tough 1993 legislation that left some immigrants in a legal limbo -- some with children born in France can neither be deported nor obtain legal status.
